[![](https://img.shields.io/badge/doi-10.1137%2F1.9781611975321.62-yellow)](https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9781611975321.62 ) 39: 40: The framework uses a notion of a leader as an individual who initiates collective patterns that everyone in a group follows. 41: 42: Given a set of time series of individual activities, our goal is to identify periods of coordinated activity, find factions of coordination if more than one exist, as well as identify leaders of each faction. 43: 44: For each time step, the framework infers following relations between individual time series, then identifying a leader of each faction whom many individuals follow but it follows no one. A faction is defined as a group of individuals that everyone follows the same leader. 45: 46: mFLICA reports following relations, leaders of factions, and members of each faction for each time step. 47: 48: Installation 49: ------------ 50: You can install our package from CRAN 51: 52: ```r 53: install.packages("mFLICA") 54: ``` 55: 56: For the newest version on github, please call the following command in R terminal. 57: 58: ``` r 59: remotes::install_github("DarkEyes/mFLICA") 60: ``` 61: This requires a user to install the "remotes" package before installing mFLICA. 62: 63: EXAMPLE 64: ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 65: 66: In the first step, we have a build-in dataset of 30-individual time series where ID1, ID2, and ID3 are leaders at coordination intervals: [1,200], [201,400], and [401,600] respectively. These individuals move within two-dimensional space. Time series of each individual represents a sequence of coordinate (x,y) at each time step. A leader is an initiator who initiates coordinated movement that everyone in a faction follows. 67: 68: ```{r} 69: library(mFLICA) 70: 71: # mFLICA::TS[i,t,d] is an element of ith time series at time t in the dimension d. Here, we have only two dimensions: x and y. The time series length is 800, so, t is in the range [1,800]. There are 30 individuals, so, i is in the range [1,30]. 72: plotMultipleTimeSeries(TS=mFLICA::TS[,,1],strTitle="x axis") 73: ``` 74: 75: 76: ```{r} 77: plotMultipleTimeSeries(TS=mFLICA::TS[,,2],strTitle="y axis") 78: ``` 79: 80: 81: The framework is used to analyze the data below. 82: ```{r} 83: obj1<-mFLICA(TS=mFLICA::TS[,1:800,],timeWindow=60,sigma=0.5) 84: ``` 85: The network densities of a dynamic following network is shown below. At any time step t, a higher network density implies a higher degree of coordination; the higher number of individuals that follow the same pattern with some time delays. 86: ```{r} 87: plotMultipleTimeSeries(TS=obj1$dyNetOut$dyNetBinDensityVec, strTitle="Network Dnesity") 88: ``` 89: 90: 91: We plot time series of faction size ratios of all leaders. A faction size ratio is just a network density calculating from only edges within a faction leading by a specific leader. If everyone follows a single leader, then a faction size ratio is the same as the network density, which has the value at one. 92: ```{r} 93: plotMultipleTimeSeries(TS=obj1$factionSizeRatioTimeSeries, strTitle="Faction Size Ratios") 94: ``` 95: 96: 97: Here, we know that ID1, ID2, and ID3 are leaders at coordination intervals: [1,200], [201,400], and [401,600] respectively. Hence, ID1, ID2 and ID3 have their faction size ratios being high during the intervals that they lead the group. 98: 99: Citation 100: ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 101: Amornbunchornvej, Chainarong, and Tanya Y. Berger-Wolf. "Framework for Inferring Leadership Dynamics of Complex Movement from Time Series." In Proceedings of the 2018 SIAM International Conference on Data Mining (SDM), pp. 549-557. **Assessing HTML and execution around R scripts**

I’m contemplating generating minimal HTML to show the output under results, but actual execution of chunks is still essential for evidence. I wonder if using `knitr::knit` and `markdownToHTML` in a script could be the way to go, though it might take a bit. Maybe I should create a custom R script to handle this while considering whether to run it with `eval=FALSE`. Checking if the results directory is empty leads me to think that manually combining code and outputs could be a workaround.

I want to create a minimal HTML file that includes both the source code and outputs, but it might not require the exact notebook format. I can include small evaluated objects for evidence, yet I still need to generate that HTML without running heavy code chunks. Although there was an issue with rendering due to pandoc, I think I can use `knitr::knit` and `markdown::markdownToHTML`. I'll write a script to run with `Rscript`, aiming to finish within a reasonable timeout—maybe around 10 seconds!

**Exploring timeout solutions for R scripts**

I’m thinking that maybe the command times out because there’s no output. To prevent this, I might consider using a `timeout` shell command, but that doesn't feel quite right. A background process could work, but then the tool might still wait. Ah, using `nohup` could be the trick! I could launch the long-running R script in the background and poll it until it finishes. I’ll create a script to knit and convert, keeping an eye on the timeout. Sounds good!
